Personal project

Credit Risk Analysis

  • Python
  • SQL
  • Tableau
  • Logistic regression
  • 1.34M loans
  • 0.69 AUC
  • 55% of defaults caught
Problem
Which borrowers are likely to default, and how should a lender prioritize who to review?
Data
LendingClub loan data from Kaggle, 2.26M loans narrowed down to 1.34M with a clear outcome (paid off or charged off)
My role
Built the whole project myself, including the cleaning, database, SQL, model, and dashboard
Approach
Cleaned the data in pandas, loaded it into a SQL database with SQLAlchemy, and used SQL to build a simple FICO based tier as a baseline. Then trained a logistic regression model on 6 features (loan amount, interest rate, FICO, debt to income, income, past delinquencies) with an 80/20 split, and grouped borrowers into tiers by the model's predicted default probability, using the same tier sizes as FICO so the two could be compared fairly
Result
0.69 AUC. On 269K test loans, the model's high risk tier defaulted at 32.2% and caught 55% of all defaults, compared with 25.0% and 43% for the FICO tier of the same size. The model's low risk tier defaulted at only 6.7%, vs. 11.7% for FICO. Interest rate was the strongest predictor, followed by income
Takeaway
A bank should tier borrowers by the model score, not FICO alone, and not lend to everyone on the same terms. The model's low risk group (6.7% default rate) can be approved quickly at standard rates. The medium group could still be approved, but with a slightly higher rate or a smaller loan. The high risk group defaults almost 1 in 3 times, so those loans should get a closer review, a higher rate, a lower limit, or be declined

Personal project

Job Intel Agent

  • Python
  • SQLAlchemy
  • REST APIs
  • OAuth 2.0
  • Claude API
  • 12K postings per run
  • 1.00 precision on 25 tests
  • $2.91 per 1K jobs
Problem
Job searching is repetitive and takes too much time, and many postings don't fit an entry level analyst. How much of that can be automated?
Data
Postings from public company job boards, public job listing repositories on GitHub, and my Gmail, which I use to track the companies I already applied to
My role
Building it myself as a personal project
Approach
A Python service finds which job board platform each company uses, pulls postings through REST APIs and OAuth 2.0, and stores them with SQLAlchemy. Claude Haiku then checks each posting (is it early career? is it an analytics role?) and scores the fit from 1 to 10 with a short reason
Result
A normal run pulls about 12,000 raw postings from company job boards (12,901, 12,170, and 12,288 on three normal runs in September), and the filters cut that down to about 65 to 80 roles worth scoring. So far it has collected 29,700+ postings from 700+ companies. On a hand labeled test set of 25 postings, both classifiers scored 1.00 precision and recall, and 24 of 25 fit scores landed in the expected range, at about $2.91 per 1,000 jobs
Takeaway
Replaces manual job board searching with one ranked daily report of roles that actually fit

Team class project

NYC 311 Noise & Weather Warehouse

  • Alteryx
  • BigQuery
  • SQL
  • Tableau
  • 500K complaints
  • 9 BigQuery tables
  • Peak at 60 to 70°F
Problem
Does the weather affect how many noise complaints New Yorkers make to 311? Our guess was that warm days bring more people outside and more complaints, while cold, rainy, or snowy days bring fewer.
Data
500,000 noise complaints from NYC Open Data's 311 Service Requests, joined with NOAA daily weather from NYC stations (high and low temperature, rain, snow, and wind), covering March 2020 to March 2026
My role
Team class project. I built the integrated data marts, the Alteryx ETL workflow, and the BigQuery tables, and made the temperature KPI. I also worked on the proposal and the final data model with the team
Approach
Cleaned and standardized both datasets in Alteryx, then loaded them straight into BigQuery as 9 tables. The 311 fact table has one row per complaint with its response time in hours, and the weather fact table has one row per station per day. Both connect through a shared date table. Then wrote SQL in BigQuery for each KPI and made the charts in Tableau
Result
My KPI showed an inverted U. Complaints rise from cold to mild weather, peak around 60 to 70°F, then drop on the hottest days. Every borough had the most complaints on hot, dry days and the fewest on snowy days, and weekends had almost twice as many complaints as Monday to Thursday
Takeaway
Weather and noise complaints are related, but not in a straight line. Very hot and very cold days both seem to keep people inside, and the day of the week matters too, since people go out more at the end of the week
